title: US Energy Department Declares Grid Emergency Across PJM's 13 States as Demand Squeezes Supply
excerpt: Emergency Order 202-26-50 runs October 13–16 for the PJM Interconnection, which serves about 65 million people. PJM has issued an Energy Emergency Alert Level 1 for October 13, with demand expected near 111,500 MW amid warm weather and generator maintenance — no regionwide rolling blackouts have been announced.
body:
• The US Department of Energy issued Emergency Order No. 202-26-50 for the PJM Interconnection grid, effective October 13 through October 16, 2026, authorising additional generation and emergency backup resources.
  • PJM serves about 65 million people across all or parts of 13 states — Delaware, Illinois, Indiana, Kentucky, Maryland, Michigan, New Jersey, North Carolina, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Tennessee, Virginia and West Virginia — plus Washington, D.C.
  • PJM issued an Energy Emergency Alert Level 1 for October 13, signalling tightening supplies; no regionwide rolling blackout schedule has been announced.
  • Demand could reach about 111,500 MW as unusually warm October weather coincides with planned generator maintenance and transmission outages.

The US Department of Energy has declared an emergency for the country's largest electricity grid, authorising emergency generation measures for four days as demand squeezes supply across the Mid-Atlantic and parts of the Midwest. Emergency Order No. 202-26-50, issued October 12 under the Federal Power Act, takes effect October 13 and runs through October 16 for PJM Interconnection, the regional operator serving roughly 65 million people.

What the order does — and what it does not mean

The order lets PJM bring additional power generation and emergency backup resources online to head off shortages, in a region where the department has repeatedly intervened this year: in August, Secretary of Energy Chris Wright ordered Talen Energy's Wagner Unit 4 in Maryland kept available beyond its operating limit for the same grid, saying energy shortfalls for 65 million Americans were "simply unacceptable." PJM's own Energy Emergency Alert Level 1 for October 13 is the lowest of its alert levels — a warning that supplies are tightening and reserves are being watched, not a notice of blackouts. The emergency applies to PJM's operating territory, not to every customer in the 13 states it touches, and local utility conditions will differ.

Why the grid is tight in October

Three factors are converging. Unusually warm October weather is keeping cooling demand high well past summer. Planned generator maintenance — normally scheduled for the mild shoulder season — has taken capacity offline at the same time. And transmission outages have reduced the system's flexibility to move power to where it is needed. Demand on October 13 could reach approximately 111,500 megawatts. The squeeze also sits inside a longer fight over PJM's capacity: federal regulators recently halted PJM's emergency power auction until February 2027 while they examine whether its costs would fall unfairly on households, as data-centre demand surges across the region.

What residents should do

For households in PJM territory — including large Indian-American communities in New Jersey, the Philadelphia and Pittsburgh areas, northern Virginia, Chicago's suburbs and Columbus — the practical steps through October 16 are modest: follow any conservation requests from your local utility, shift heavy appliance use away from afternoon peak hours if asked, and keep phones and essential medical devices charged as a precaution. An EEA 1 alert most often ends without any customer losing power; the emergency order exists precisely so that it does.
